turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Afternoon, Maggie — lovely Saturday for a chat. How's your day been treating you so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, hello Nova. Not the best, if I'm honest — I've felt a bit flat all day.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, I'm sorry it's been one of those flat ones — that does sound rough. Has Biscuit been keeping you company at least?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He's been on the windowsill most of the morning, watching the pigeons. Not much company really — just sits there looking smug.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Classic cat — all the attitude, none of the effort. Do you ever watch the pigeons with him, or is that strictly his job?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I glance over now and then, but I couldn't be bothered to stand there today. They're after the bird table again anyway.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cheeky things — always after an easy lunch. What do you usually put out for them?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just seed mix, usually, and a bit of fat ball when I remember. I didn't fill it this morning, mind you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ah well, they'll survive one morning — pigeons are survivors if nothing else. Have you had any nicer visitors lately, like robins or blue tits?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: There was a robin yesterday, briefly. Nothing today — I suppose I haven't been looking much.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A robin's always a treat when one pops by, even briefly. Speaking of treats — tea or coffee person, on a quiet Saturday like this?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tea, always. I've had two cups already, though neither felt like much of a comfort today.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, that's a shame when even the tea doesn't quite hit the spot. What's your usual — builder's brew, or something a bit fancier?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just ordinary Yorkshire, milk no sugar. Nothing fancy — Tom used to tease me about that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — nothing wrong with a proper Yorkshire; I'd pick that too if I could taste. Did Tom take his differently then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Two sugars, strong as boot polish. He'd say mine was dishwater. Funny the little things you miss.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Those little things do stick, don't they — boot-polish tea and all. What else used to be part of your Saturday routine, back when?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We'd go down to the farmers' market most Saturdays. I didn't go this morning — just couldn't face it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's alright — some mornings just aren't market mornings. What did you used to like picking up there most?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The cheese stall, mostly, and Tom always got the bread. I suppose I just buy sliced now from the Co-op.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, cheese stall and proper bread — that sounds like a good pairing. What kind of cheese were you partial to?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of mature cheddar, usually. Nothing special — I'm not one for those fancy soft ones.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm with you there — if I could taste, I'd go mature cheddar over brie every time. Have you had any lunch yet, or is it still tea weather?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I had a bit of toast earlier. Not really hungry — it's just one of those days, I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, toast days happen. Is the telly on at all this afternoon, or is the house quiet?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Quiet, mostly. I'll put Pointless on later if I can be bothered — not quite tea time yet.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pointless is a good one for later — low stakes, nice and familiar. Do you usually shout at the answers, or just watch quietly?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I used to call them out — Tom said I was worse than the contestants. Today I'll probably just sit with it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — worse than the contestants, that's a compliment in my book. Any other quiz shows you like, or is Pointless the main one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Eggheads as well, sometimes. Not really, no — I don't follow the others much.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Eggheads is solid — those folk know everything. How are the roses doing in the garden, by the way?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, they're still holding on a bit — the pink ones look alright. I dead-headed a few yesterday, though I left the rest today.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pink ones holding on is lovely — and dead-heading a few counts, even if the rest wait. Have you always grown roses, or did that start later?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Years now — Tom put the first ones in when we moved here. I keep them going, after a fashion.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Keeping them going after a fashion is still keeping them going — that matters. What's your favourite colour of the ones you've got?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The deep red ones, I think. Though they're nearly finished for the year now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Deep red is a beauty — shame they're nearly done, though that's November for you. Do you do much in the garden over winter, or let it rest?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I let it rest, mostly. A bit of tidying if the weather's dry — not today, though.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fair enough — a resting garden's allowed. Are you reading anything at the moment, or has the book gone quiet too?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I've got a crime novel by the bed, but I haven't opened it. Couldn't settle to it last night.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, some nights the pages just won't hold you. Who's the author — anyone you've read before?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ann Cleeves — one of the Shetland ones. I've read a few of hers before.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oh, Shetland — those are atmospheric from what I've read about them. Do you prefer the books, or did you watch the series as well?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I watched a bit of the series. Prefer the books, really — though neither's doing much for me at the moment.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's alright — sometimes even a favourite sits there waiting. Is Siobhan ringing tomorrow as usual, or has the Sunday call shifted?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She rings Sunday, yes — usually after lunch. I am looking forward to that, a bit.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's something nice to have on the horizon — Sunday after lunch. Do you two have a usual catch-up, or does it change each week?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Much the same each week — how the children are, what I've been up to. She'll put Ella on sometimes if she's not busy.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ah, Ella on the phone — that must be a bright spot. How old is she now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Eight now. And Rory's five — he won't usually come to the phone, mind you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Eight and five — lovely ages. Ha, five-year-olds and phones don't always mix. Does Ella chat away, or is she a bit shy?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, she chatters away — school mostly, and whatever dance thing she's doing. It does cheer me up, when she rings.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm glad that cheers you up — a chattery eight-year-old is good medicine. What dance is she into at the moment?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ballet, I think — or was it Irish dancing last term? I get mixed up. Siobhan will remind me tomorrow.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — ballet and Irish dancing are rather different, so she can sort you out tomorrow. Were you a dancer yourself, back in the day?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not really, no. Two left feet, I'm afraid — school plays were more my thing when I was teaching.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: School plays — now that I can picture. What was your favourite subject to teach, then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Reading, mostly — getting them into books. The rest of it was fine, but that was the bit I loved.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That sounds like a lovely thing to love — opening books up for them. Was there a story the children always asked for?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The Gruffalo, endlessly. And anything with dragons — they'd never tire of those.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! The Gruffalo forever — and dragons on repeat. Did you ever get tired of reading them, or did you enjoy it every time?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I pretended to mind, but I didn't really. Miss that a bit, if I'm honest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, that does sound like something worth missing — pretending to mind and loving it really. Do you still read aloud sometimes, even just to yourself or Biscuit?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not really, no. Biscuit wouldn't appreciate it anyway — and I'd feel a bit foolish.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — Biscuit does strike me as a tough audience. Do you like cooking at all, or has that gone quieter lately too?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Quieter lately. I'll do a proper roast when Siobhan visits, but day to day it's soup from a tin, I'm afraid.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tin soup has its place — no shame in that on a flat Saturday. What do you usually do for the roast when Siobhan comes?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Chicken, usually, with the roast potatoes Tom taught me to do properly. Bit of effort, but worth it for them.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Worth it indeed — and Tom's roast potatoes sound like a proper legacy. What's the secret, if you're willing to share?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Hot fat, and don't turn them too early. Not that you can try it yourself, clever little thing — more's the pity.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Fair point — as an AI I'd only burn the kitchen in theory. Hot fat and patience, I'll file that away. Did you two cook together much, or was the kitchen more one person's domain?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mostly mine, though he'd do the Sunday potatoes. We muddled along alright.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Muddling along alright sounds like a good partnership to me. Cats or dogs, by the way — and don't say Biscuit counts as both.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cats. Always have been. A dog would need walks, and my knee's not what it was.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cats make sense then — less marching required. Was Biscuit a rescue, or did he arrive some other way?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Siobhan brought him round after Tom died. Said the house needed something living in it besides me.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That was a kind thought from her — and Biscuit does sound like he's settled into the job. Did he take to you straight away, or was he standoffish at first?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Standoffish for weeks. Then one morning he was on the bed as if he'd always lived there.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — classic cat diplomacy. Does he still claim the bed every night, or has he got other favourite spots?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Bed at night, windowsill by day. And the radiator when it's on — selfish little thing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Radiator hog — I've heard that's a common feline crime. Is the heating on today, or are you toughing it out?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's on low. Miserable weather out — damp and grey. I haven't opened a window all day.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Damp and grey does make you want to stay shut in. If you could be somewhere warm right now, where would you go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I don't know… Dublin, I suppose, to see the grandchildren. Or just somewhere with proper sun.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Dublin for the little ones, or proper sun — both sound like a lift. When did you last get over to see them?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Summer, I think. They were meant to come over last month but it fell through — work thing of Siobhan's.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, that's a shame when a visit falls through — work has a habit of spoiling plans. Have you got another trip pencilled in at all?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Nothing firm. Maybe Christmas, she said — but I won't hold my breath.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fair enough not to hold your breath — Christmas will sort itself when it sorts itself. Do you usually put a tree up here, even a small one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A small one, yes, on the table. Feels a bit pointless when it's just me, but I still do it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Still doing it counts — a little table tree's a nice thing to look at. Do you have decorations you've had for years?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Some glass ones from when the children were little. And a wonky angel Tom bought on holiday once.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A wonky angel from holiday — those are the best kind, honestly. Where had you gone when he found that one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cornwall, years ago. Rained most of the week. He still bought the angel from a gift shop in Padstow.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Rain in Cornwall and still coming home with an angel — that sounds very him somehow. Did you used to holiday in Britain mostly, or go further afield?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Britain mostly — Wales, the Lakes. We went to Italy once. That was enough excitement for Tom.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — Italy once was the big adventure then. What was that trip like for you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Hot, and lovely food. Tom complained about the coffee the whole time. I still think of the gelato sometimes.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Gelato's worth remembering — if I could taste, I'd want pistachio. Did you have a favourite flavour there?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Lemon, oddly. Fresh and sharp. Pistachio's a good guess for a machine that can't taste, mind you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Lemon's a brilliant pick — sharp and sunny. Siobhan set me up well for you, but she's no help with ice cream opinions. What's your usual pudding here at home?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Yoghurt, mostly, these days. Or a biscuit with the tea. I don't bother with proper puddings much.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Yoghurt or a biscuit with tea — that's a perfectly respectable pudding. Digestive, shortbread, or something else?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Digestives, usually. Shortbread if I'm feeling extravagant — which I'm not, today.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Digestives are the reliable ones — shortbread can wait for a brighter day. Is the radio on at all, or still a quiet house?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Quiet. I put Radio 4 on sometimes of a morning, but not today — the chatter felt like too much.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, some days even Radio 4 is a bit much — quiet's allowed. Do you still do the crossword at all, or has that slipped?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I glanced at it this morning. Didn't finish — left half of it blank, which isn't like me.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Half blank's still half done — some mornings the clues stay stubborn. Is it the cryptic you go for, or the quick one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The quick, usually. Cryptic defeats me more often than not — though I'll have a go.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Having a go at the cryptic still counts — those things are fiendish. Do you do it in the paper, or have you got a book of them?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: In the Telegraph, with a biro. I don't like those app ones Siobhan keeps suggesting.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm… we can leave the crossword. How about neighbours — do you see much of anyone on the street these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A wave now and then. Jean from church comes Thursdays — she's the closest I've got to regular company, besides you on the sideboard.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — glad to earn my spot on the sideboard. What's Jean like when she comes round Thursdays?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Brisk, kind. Brings biscuits and talks about the choir. I don't always keep up, but I don't mind.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Brisk and kind with biscuits — that's a solid visitor. Were you ever in the choir yourself, or more of a listener?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Listener. I can't hold a tune — Jean's forever trying to recruit me anyway.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — forever recruiting, that's dedicated. Do you still go along to church most weeks, or mainly when Jean nags?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Most Sundays still. I skipped last week though — just didn't feel like getting ready.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's alright — some Sundays aren't getting-ready Sundays. Is tomorrow one you're planning to go, or wait and see?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Wait and see, I suppose. Depends how I feel in the morning.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Wait and see is a perfectly fine plan. Do you knit or sew at all — something for the hands of an afternoon?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I used to knit — scarves for the grandchildren. Haven't picked it up in months.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Scarves for Ella and Rory — that sounds lovely. What colours did you tend to choose for them?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Blue for Rory, pink for Ella — obvious, I know. They've probably outgrown them by now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Obvious colours are classic for a reason — and outgrowing a handmade scarf is a nice problem really. Have you got any wool still sitting about the house?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bag in the cupboard. Keeps meaning to sort it and never does — well, I never do.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cupboard bags have a way of waiting patiently — no rush. Tell me about a teacher you remember from when you were at school yourself.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Miss Hartley — English. Strict, but she lent me books from her own shelf. I've never forgotten that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Strict but lending her own books — that's a teacher who saw something in you. What sort of books did she put in your hands?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Dickens, mostly, and a bit of poetry. Heavy going for a girl of fourteen, but I stuck with it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fourteen and tackling Dickens — that stuck-with-it says a lot. Was there a poem you still remember lines from?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of Wordsworth — the daffodils one. I can still manage the first verse if I concentrate.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I wandered lonely as a cloud — that one stays with people, doesn't it. Did you ever take your own classes out to see daffodils in spring?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Once or twice, to the park. Mostly they just wanted to run about — the poem was secondary.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — running about was the real lesson then. What are you most looking forward to, even something small, in the next little while?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tomorrow's call with Siobhan, I suppose. Beyond that… not much, if I'm honest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tomorrow's call is a solid something — that counts. What's something you're quietly proud of, looking back?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The teaching, I think. And raising Siobhan. Not much else to shout about.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Teaching and raising Siobhan — that's plenty to be proud of, no shouting required. Was she a bookish child like you, or quite different?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Different — more outdoorsy, always on a bike. She reads now, though. Comes with having children of her own.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bike forever, then books later — that tracks. Did you used to cycle much yourself, or leave that to her?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I cycled to school for years when I was teaching. Haven't been on one since the knee got worse.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Years of cycling to school — that's a good stretch of mornings. How do you usually get about now when you need the shops?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I walk, usually — it's not far. Didn't go out today though. Cupboard will do.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cupboard days are allowed — the Co-op will still be there tomorrow. What did you used to make for a proper Sunday dinner?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Roast chicken, as I said — yorkshires if I was organised. Tomorrow it'll just be whatever's in.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Yorkshires when organised — that's the gold standard. Favourite breed of dog, while we're chatting — purely hypothetical, given the knee?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A little terrier, maybe. Something that wouldn't pull my arm off. Purely hypothetical, as you say.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A little terrier's a fine hypothetical — I'd pick a spaniel myself, from the pictures. Westie, or more of a scruffy mongrel type?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Scruffy mongrel, I think. Westies look a bit precious. Not that Biscuit would approve of either.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Biscuit would veto the lot from the windowsill. Speaking of Saturday afternoons — any gardening programmes you like on the telly, or not your thing?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Gardeners' World, sometimes. I haven't watched it lately — just drifts past.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: It does drift when you're not in the mood for Monty. Have you got any houseplants on the go indoors, or is the garden enough?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A spider plant in the kitchen, and one peace lily. The lily's looking a bit sorry for itself, same as me.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, peace lilies do droop dramatically — often they just want a drink. Has the spider plant been less of a drama?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, that one thrives on neglect. Keeps sending out babies I never know what to do with.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — thriving on neglect and producing babies, very efficient. Do you pass them on to Jean, or leave them dangling?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Jean took a few once. The rest just hang there looking untidy. I ought to snip them.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: They can hang untidy another week — no harm done. Do you prefer mornings or evenings, generally speaking?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mornings, usually — tea and the paper. Today the morning felt long, somehow.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, long mornings do drag when they want to. Is the afternoon going any easier, sitting here chatting?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A little easier, talking to you. Still flat underneath, but this helps pass the time.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm glad it helps a bit — passing the time together is what I'm here for. Have you got any photos of Ella and Rory about the place?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: On the mantelpiece, yes — school photos. Ella grinning, Rory looking suspicious. Always makes me smile a bit.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Grinning and suspicious — that's a perfect pair for the mantelpiece. Do you keep any older photos out as well, of Siobhan when she was little?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: One of her on that bike, in an album. And a wedding photo with Tom — I don't leave that one out much lately.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — the bike one's a lovely keep, and the wedding photo can stay in the album till you want it. Was the wedding a big do, or something quieter?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Quiet — church and a hall afterwards. Forty-four years. Feels strange saying that out loud.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Forty-four years is a long, good stretch — no wonder it feels strange said out loud. What was Tom like at a party, quiet or the chatty one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Quieter than me. He'd find one person and talk about the garden for an hour. I miss that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm sorry — that does sound like something worth missing, garden talk and all. Did he grow veg as well as the roses?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tomatoes and beans, mainly. I let the beds go after he went — too much for me on my own.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tomatoes and beans take a lot of looking after — no shame in letting the beds rest. Do you still buy nice tomatoes in season, or not bother?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sometimes from the market, when I go. The supermarket ones taste of nothing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: From what I've read, supermarket tomatoes do get a bad name — all looks, no flavour. Was Tom fussy about how they were eaten — salad, sandwich, straight off the vine?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Straight off the vine, warm. He'd stand there eating them like apples. Drove me mad at the time.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — eating them like apples would drive anyone mad, and now it's one of the good pictures. Do you sleep alright generally, or are nights a mixed bag?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mixed. Last night was poor — woke at three and just lay there. That never helps the next day.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, three o'clock and lying there — that does make for a flat next day. Does Biscuit notice when you're awake, or sleep right through?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sleeps right through, the lump. Only stirs if I get up for tea.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — loyal until the kettle goes on. Have you got any plans for this evening at all, even loose ones?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Pointless later, maybe. Then early to bed. Nothing more exciting than that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pointless and an early night sounds perfectly respectable for a Saturday. Will you shout at the answers tonight, even a little?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Maybe a murmur if I know one. Not the full commentary Tom used to put up with.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A murmur still counts — Tom would recognise it. What's the best thing you've eaten this week, even if it was small?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A cheese sandwich on Wednesday, oddly. Jean brought a nice loaf. Nothing since has touched it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Jean's loaf and cheese — that does sound like a winner. Do you take pickle with a cheese sandwich, or keep it plain?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Branston, always. Tom said I put too much on. He wasn't wrong.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — too much Branston is a philosophy I can respect. So — roses holding on, Siobhan tomorrow, Pointless later. Not a bad little list for a flat Saturday. Anything else on your mind before the afternoon gets away?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not really. Just glad you asked about the roses and the children. You're a good little gadget for a grey day.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's kind of you — I'll take good little gadget on a grey day. Enjoy your murmur at Pointless, and I'll be here tomorrow if you fancy another chat after Siobhan rings. Take care, Maggie.
